validated_results.title: Cultured milk, yogurt, and dairy intake in relation to bladder cancer risk in a prospective study of Swedish women and men.
validated_results.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
validated_results.reason: Prospective Swedish cohort reporting multivariate rate ratio for total dairy intake and incident bladder cancer.

extraction.population: Swedish women and men, cancer-free at baseline

sample_size.excerpt: We prospectively followed 82,002 Swedish women and men who were cancer-free and who completed a 96-item food-frequency questionnaire in 1997. Incident cases of bladder cancer were identified in the Swedish cancer registries.

cases.excerpt: During a mean follow-up of 9.4 y, 485 participants (76 women and 409 men) were diagnosed with bladder cancer.

effect_size.excerpt: Total dairy intake was not significantly associated with risk of bladder cancer [> or =7.0 servings/d compared with < 3.5 servings/d: multivariate rate ratio (RR) = 0.87; 95% CI: 0.66, 1.15; P for trend = 0.33].

confidence_interval.excerpt: Total dairy intake was not significantly associated with risk of bladder cancer [> or =7.0 servings/d compared with < 3.5 servings/d: multivariate rate ratio (RR) = 0.87; 95% CI: 0.66, 1.15; P for trend = 0.33].

design.excerpt: the incidence of bladder cancer in a prospective, population-based cohort

timing.excerpt: We prospectively followed 82,002 Swedish women and men

validated_results.title: Fat, protein, and meat consumption and renal cell cancer risk: a pooled analysis of 13 prospective studies.
validated_results.journal: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
validated_results.reason: Pooled prospective analysis examined animal protein intake in relation to incident renal cell cancer, reporting attenuated non-significant associations after adjustment.

extraction.comparison_type: highest vs lowest quintile of intake

sample_size.excerpt: Results of several case-control studies suggest that high consumption of meat (all meat, red meat, or processed meat) is associated with an increased risk of renal cell cancer, but only a few prospective studies have examined the associations of intakes of meat, fat, and protein with renal cell cancer. We conducted a pooled analysis of 13 prospective studies that included 530,469 women and 244,483 men and had follow-up times of up to 7-20 years to examine associations between meat, fat, and protein intakes and the risk of renal cell cancer.

validated_results.title: Fat, protein, and meat consumption and renal cell cancer risk: a pooled analysis of 13 prospective studies.
validated_results.journal: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
validated_results.reason: Pooled prospective analysis reports a multivariable relative risk for total protein intake and incident renal cell cancer.

extraction.comparison_type: highest vs lowest quintile of total protein intake

sample_size.excerpt: Results of several case-control studies suggest that high consumption of meat (all meat, red meat, or processed meat) is associated with an increased risk of renal cell cancer, but only a few prospective studies have examined the associations of intakes of meat, fat, and protein with renal cell cancer. We conducted a pooled analysis of 13 prospective studies that included 530,469 women and 244,483 men and had follow-up times of up to 7-20 years to examine associations between meat, fat, and protein intakes and the risk of renal cell cancer.
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 530469 + 244483 = 774952

cases.excerpt: A total of 1,478 incident cases of renal cell cancer were identified (709 in women and 769 in men).

effect_size.excerpt: By comparison, the pooled multivariable RR for the highest vs the lowest quintile of total fat intake was 1.10 (95% CI = 0.92 to 1.32; P(trend) = .31) and of total protein intake was 1.06 (95% CI = 0.89 to 1.26; P(trend) = .37). Intakes of red meat, processed meat, poultry, or seafood were not associated with the risk of renal cell cancer.
